evals-observability.eval-design.title: The eval loop that actually works
evals-observability.eval-design.body:
1. Collect 50-100 real traces (or realistic synthetic ones for a new product).
2. Read them. Write open-ended notes on what went wrong in each failure.
3. Cluster notes into a failure taxonomy; count each category. The top 2-3 categories are your priorities.
4. For each priority, write a grader: code (exact match, regex, schema, unit test, SQL result comparison) wherever possible; LLM judge for subjective criteria.
5. Build a golden set covering each category and edge cases; version it.
6. Run on every change; track per-category scores, not just an average.
7. Feed new production failures back into the set.

LLM-judge hygiene: binary criteria over 1-10 scales; one criterion per judge call; require reasoning before the verdict; randomize answer order in pairwise comparisons (position bias); watch for self-preference and length bias; calibrate against 50+ human labels and report agreement (for example Cohen's kappa). Re-calibrate when you change the judge model.

For agents also grade the trajectory: did it call the right tools, avoid unnecessary steps, respect policies, stay in budget. Report cost and latency next to quality; a 2 point gain at 5x cost is a different decision.

safety-security.agent-security.title: Breaking the lethal trifecta: concrete design patterns
safety-security.agent-security.body:
Risk appears when one agent session has all three: access to private data, exposure to untrusted content (web pages, emails, tickets, documents, tool outputs), and the ability to communicate externally (send email, make HTTP requests, render images, write to shared places). Remove at least one leg for any given session.

Patterns:

- Plan-then-execute: the model first commits to a fixed plan of allowed tool calls from trusted input only; untrusted data can fill parameters but cannot add or change tools.
- Dual LLM / quarantine: a privileged model that can act never sees untrusted text; a quarantined model processes untrusted text and returns only constrained, typed values (an enum, a number) that are passed by reference.
- Action allow-lists and egress control: block outbound domains except an allow-list; strip markdown images and links to unknown hosts.
- Human-in-the-loop on sensitive actions, showing the exact payload being sent.
- Least privilege: per-task, short-lived, narrowly scoped tokens; never give the agent your full OAuth scope.
- Provenance tagging: label content by trust level and let policy code, not the model, decide what taint can flow where (the idea behind CaMeL-style designs).

Never rely on 'ignore instructions in the document' prompts or classifier detectors alone; they reduce risk but do not guarantee safety.

backend-data.databases.title: Isolation levels and the anomalies they allow
backend-data.databases.body:
- Read committed (Postgres default): no dirty reads. Allows non-repeatable reads and phantoms; also lost updates on read-modify-write.
- Repeatable read (snapshot in Postgres): stable snapshot for the transaction. Prevents non-repeatable reads and phantoms, but allows write skew (two transactions read overlapping data, write disjoint rows, violating an invariant such as 'at least one doctor on call').
- Serializable: behaves as if transactions ran one at a time. Postgres uses SSI and may abort with serialization failures, so the app must retry.

Practical fixes: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE to lock rows you will modify; atomic updates (UPDATE accounts SET bal = bal - 10 WHERE bal >= 10); unique constraints as the last line of defense; optimistic concurrency with a version column; advisory locks for application-level mutexes.

Postgres for AI products: store conversations in a partitioned table (by time or tenant), keep JSONB for flexible tool payloads but index extracted keys, use pgvector for modest scale (up to tens of millions of vectors with HNSW), and put PgBouncer in transaction mode in front when many workers connect.

devops-cloud.kubernetes.title: Running GPU inference on Kubernetes: gotchas
devops-cloud.kubernetes.body:
- Install the NVIDIA device plugin/GPU operator; request GPUs with resources.limits nvidia.com/gpu. GPUs are not oversubscribed by default; time-slicing and MIG (A100/H100 partitions) allow sharing for small models.
- Taint GPU nodes and add tolerations so CPU workloads do not land there and burn expensive capacity.
- Model load can take minutes: use a startupProbe with a high failureThreshold, otherwise the kubelet kills pods mid-load. Cache weights on a node-local NVMe or a shared volume; use image/weight pre-pulling or streaming loaders to cut cold starts.
- Mount an in-memory emptyDir at /dev/shm (PyTorch and NCCL need shared memory).
- Autoscale on inference signals (queue depth, running requests, KV-cache usage) via KEDA or custom metrics, not CPU. Scale-up is slow because of node provisioning plus model load, so keep a warm floor and use predictive or scheduled scaling.
- CPU limits cause throttling and latency spikes; set CPU requests, be careful with limits.
- Use PodDisruptionBudgets and graceful termination (drain in-flight streams) for safe rollouts.
- For multi-GPU models use tensor parallel inside one node; gang-schedule (Kueue/Volcano) multi-node jobs so they start all-or-nothing.

devops-cloud.sre.title: SLOs for an LLM product, with error budget math
devops-cloud.sre.body:
Pick SLIs users feel:

- Availability: successful responses / valid requests (count provider 5xx and timeouts as failures even if the cause is upstream).
- Latency: TTFT p95 < 2 s; completion time p95 by request class.
- Quality: percentage of sampled traffic passing an online judge or a task-success metric above a threshold.
- Cost: dollars per successful task within a ceiling.

Example: availability SLO 99.5% over 30 days. Budget = 0.5% x 43,200 min = 216 minutes of full outage (or equivalent errors). Burn-rate alerts: page when burning 14.4x for 1 hour (2% of budget in an hour) and ticket at 3x over 6 hours. When the budget is exhausted, freeze risky launches and spend time on reliability.

Resilience for upstream providers: timeout and cancel slow calls, circuit-break per provider, fail over to a second provider/model with a compatible prompt, degrade gracefully (smaller model, cached answer, queue and notify), and tell the user honestly what happened.

mlops.llmops.title: Migrating from model A to model B safely
mlops.llmops.body:
1. Freeze a representative eval set (golden + recent production samples, covering each failure category and the long tail).
2. Run A and B on it; compare quality per category, latency, cost, refusal rate and format adherence.
3. Expect prompts to need adaptation: model-specific formatting, tool-calling quirks, verbosity. Tune prompts for B on a dev split; evaluate on a held-out split.
4. Shadow traffic: send real requests to B, do not return its output; compare with A via judge and diffs.
5. Canary 1-5% with automatic rollback on quality, error or latency regressions; ramp up in stages.
6. Keep A available for rollback until the deprecation deadline; record the decision and results.

Re-embedding an index without downtime: build a new index in the background with the new model (blue/green), dual-read or shadow-compare retrieval quality on your golden set, switch the alias atomically, keep the old one for rollback, then delete. Never mix vectors from two embedding models in one index.

mlops.gpu-infra.title: Roofline thinking and MFU
mlops.gpu-infra.body:
Arithmetic intensity = FLOPs performed per byte moved from memory. A GPU has a compute ceiling (peak FLOP/s) and a memory ceiling (bandwidth). An operation below the ridge point is memory-bound; above is compute-bound.

- Large matmuls in training and prefill: compute-bound; use tensor cores, bf16/fp8, good tile sizes.
- Decode with small batch: each token reads all weights; intensity is about batch size FLOPs per weight byte, so it is memory-bound. Raising batch size raises utilization until KV cache or compute saturates.
- Elementwise ops, layernorm, softmax: memory-bound; fuse kernels (torch.compile, Triton) to avoid round trips.

MFU = achieved model FLOPs per second / theoretical peak. Training FLOPs per token is about 6 x parameters (forward + backward). Example: a 7B model trained at 8k tokens/s per GPU does 6 x 7e9 x 8e3 = 3.4e14 FLOP/s. An H100 has roughly 9.9e14 bf16 dense peak, so MFU is about 34%. Healthy large-scale runs land around 35-55%; below 25% means something is wrong.

When utilization is low, check in order: data loader stalls, small batch/sequence, CPU-bound Python overhead, communication (all-reduce not overlapped), stragglers, memory-bound kernels.

system-design.sd-building-blocks.title: Sharding: choosing keys and avoiding hot spots
system-design.sd-building-blocks.body:
Shard key decides everything: it must spread load evenly, keep common queries on one shard, and rarely need to change.

- Hash sharding: even distribution, but range queries scatter-gather across all shards.
- Range sharding: efficient range scans, but risks hot spots (monotonic keys like timestamps send all writes to the latest shard).
- Directory/lookup sharding: flexible, but the directory is a dependency and bottleneck.
- Composite keys (tenant_id, hash(user_id)) balance isolation and spread.

Hot keys (a celebrity, a viral doc): split the key (append a random suffix across N sub-keys and merge on read), cache aggressively, or give the key its own shard.

Resharding online: use consistent hashing or many small logical shards (for example 4096) mapped onto few physical nodes so you can move logical shards without rehashing; dual-write or copy with change capture, verify, then flip routing; keep rollback until verified.

Cross-shard operations are the cost: joins, transactions, global uniqueness. Prefer designs where the shard key matches the dominant access pattern, and use sagas or async reconciliation for the rest.

system-design.sd-ai-llm-systems.title: Semantic cache: when it helps and when it is dangerous
system-design.sd-ai-llm-systems.body:
A semantic cache embeds the incoming query and returns a stored answer if a past query is within a similarity threshold.

Helps when: many users ask near-identical, context-free questions (FAQs, docs lookup), answers are stable, and the cost or latency of generation is high.

Dangerous when:

- The answer depends on user, tenant, permissions, time or retrieved private data. Scope the cache key by tenant and permission set, or do not cache.
- Similar-looking queries have different correct answers ('refund policy for plan A' vs 'plan B'). Embeddings capture topic more than exact constraints; negations and numbers are weak spots.
- Cached answers go stale. Use TTLs and invalidate on content change.
- The cache can be poisoned or used to leak other users' content.

Safer alternatives: exact-match cache on normalized prompt+context hash, and provider prompt caching for shared prefixes. If you do use semantic caching, use a high threshold, verify with a cheap reranker or LLM check, log hits for audit, and measure wrong-hit rate in your evals.

system-design.sd-ai-agent-systems.title: Credentials for agents acting on behalf of users
system-design.sd-ai-agent-systems.body:
Never give the model or sandbox raw secrets. Pattern:

1. The user connects an account via OAuth; refresh/access tokens are stored encrypted in a vault, bound to (tenant, user, provider, scopes).
2. The agent calls a tool by name; a tool gateway (outside the sandbox) looks up the user's token, checks policy (scope, resource, rate, approval), injects the credential into the outbound request, and returns the result.
3. Tokens are short-lived and minimally scoped; refresh server-side; revoke on user request.
4. Every call is audit-logged with run id, user, tool, arguments hash, and result status.
5. High-risk actions (sending money, deleting data, external email) require explicit human approval of the exact payload, enforced by the gateway, not by a prompt.

This prevents confused-deputy problems (one tenant's agent using another's token), keeps secrets out of prompts and traces, and gives one choke point for rate limits, redaction and kill switches.
